summary: Earth Jukebox is an accessible web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into real-time music. Instead of mapping raw colours to noise, it reads each frame's published colour bar back into the physical values scientists encoded: ocean temperature in °C, aerosol type, night-light change and forest height. It then plays those values as harmonious soundscapes, with a beam that sweeps the map from west (left ear) to east (right ear). It can calibrate itself from the colour bar of any EIC visualization. Blind and low-vision users can explore any spot by ear with the keyboard or by touch and hear it described aloud. Everyone else gets a new, emotional way to experience our planet, from the seasonal pulse of the oceans to Ukrainian cities going dark at night.
details: What it does. Earth Jukebox is an interactive web jukebox. You choose an EIC visualization and hear it as music generated live from its pixels, in any modern browser, with no install or sign-up. Four tracks: (1) Ocean Currents & Sea Surface Temperature (ECCO2, animated): pitch = water temperature (0-32 °C), timbre = cold or warm water, stereo = longitude; the background chord turns major while the northern seas are in their warm half of the year. (2) GEOS Aerosols: smoke = bass, dust = plucks, sea salt = soft tones, sulfate = bells. (3) Night Lights over Ukraine, 2012 -> 2023 (Black Marble): lit cities ring bells, dark land is silent; Dnipro, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia and Mykolaiv fall silent in 2023. (4) GEDI Forest Height: the app calibrated itself from the visualization's own colour-bar image (0-50 m). Works with any EIC visualization. Load any EIC video or image with its colour-bar picture and the two end values. Earth Jukebox finds the gradient automatically (horizontal or vertical, ignoring labels, tick marks and arrow tips), turns every pixel back into the real value (°C, m, %) and says in words what it found.How it works. Each frame is drawn onto a small hidden canvas about eight times a second. NASA colour bars become lookup tables that are inverted per pixel; grey land and black background count as no data. A radar-like beam (inspired by NASA's Caldwell 73 sonification) sweeps west to east in 16 steps and strums three latitude bands per step. Values are quantised to a D major pentatonic scale (minor for losses) and played by our own Web Audio synthesizer with a look-ahead scheduler.Accessibility (core design goal). Full keyboard control, semantic HTML, aria-live spoken updates, rich descriptions of every visualization and a written sound legend. Explore by ear turns the map into a 12x6 grid navigable by arrow keys or touch; each cell sounds its value and is read aloud. Phones vibrate more strongly for higher values. High contrast, reduced motion and forced colours are supported, and any soundscape can be recorded to an audio file.Scientific validity. Automatic calibration reproduces our hand-sampled SST table with a mean error of 0.33 °C; GEDI ticks 10/20/30/40 m read back as 10.0/20.0/30.5/40.5 m. Recovered values match known geophysics: equatorial oceans read 26-28 °C, the northern band warms from 13 °C (March) to 20 °C (September) while the southern band does the opposite; Sahara -> dust, central Africa -> smoke, Southern Ocean -> sea salt; Ukrainian cities -> much darker in 2023, Warsaw -> about the same.Why it matters. Hundreds of millions of people live with vision impairment, and NASA's Earth visualizations are closed to them. Earth Jukebox opens them up to listeners, museums like the EIC and classrooms, balancing accurate data translation with music people want to keep listening to.Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules), Web Audio API, Canvas 2D, MediaRecorder, GitHub Pages, Google Fonts. No external code libraries. Code: https://github.com/KirkaaTyapkaa/earth-jukebox
